Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 96, verses 1–19:

(p-651) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

**Tafsir (interpretation) of [Surat al-'Alaq]**

It is a Meccan surah by consensus (ijma', the agreement of scholars). It is the first part of the Book of Allah the Exalted to be revealed. Its opening was revealed in the cave of Hira', as established in Sahih al-Bukhari and elsewhere. It is narrated through Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah that "the first to be revealed was: 'O you wrapped in your garment'." Abu Maysara 'Amr ibn Shurahbil said: "The first to be revealed was the Opening of the Book (al-Fatiha)." The first view is more sound, and the sequence in the reports about the Prophet (ﷺ) requires it.

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿Recite in the name of your Lord who created.﴾ ﴿He created man from a clinging substance.﴾ ﴿Recite, and your Lord is the Most Generous.﴾ ﴿Who taught by the pen.﴾ ﴿He taught man what he did not know.﴾ ﴿No! Indeed, man transgresses.﴾ ﴿When he sees himself self-sufficient.﴾ ﴿Indeed, to your Lord is the return.﴾ ﴿Have you seen the one who forbids,﴾ ﴿a servant when he prays?﴾ ﴿Have you seen if he is upon guidance,﴾ ﴿or orders piety?﴾ ﴿Have you seen if he denies and turns away?﴾ ﴿Does he not know that Allah sees?﴾ ﴿No! If he does not desist, We will surely drag him by the forelock,﴾ ﴿a lying, sinning forelock.﴾ ﴿Then let him call his assembly;﴾ ﴿We will call the guards of Hell.﴾ ﴿No! Do not obey him, but prostrate and draw near.﴾

In Sahih al-Bukhari, from the hadith of 'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her), she said: "The first of the revelation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was true dreams. He would not see a dream except that it came like the break of dawn. Then solitude became dear to him, and he would go off to the cave of Hira' and worship there for many nights, then return to his family. Then the angel came to him while he was in the cave of Hira', and said to him: 'Recite!' He said: 'I am not one who reads.' He said: 'He seized me and pressed me, then did so three times. Then in the third time he said to him: ﴿Recite in the name of your Lord who created,﴾ ﴿He created man from a clinging substance,﴾ up to his words ﴿what he did not know.﴾'" She said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned with it, his heart trembling," and the hadith is given in full.

The meaning of this verse: "Recite this Qur'an in the name of your Lord," that is, begin your action by mentioning the name of Allah, as He the Exalted said: ﴿And he said: Embark therein; in the name of Allah is its course and its mooring﴾ [Hud: 41]. This is one interpretation. Another is in the "Book of al-Tha'labi" that the thing to be recited is "in the name of your Lord who created," as if He said to him: "Recite this phrase." When He mentioned "the Lord," and the Arabs in the Jahiliyya (pre-Islamic period) used to call idols "lords," He brought the attribute in which the idols have no share, which is His saying "who created." Then He gave them an example from created things about which there is no dispute, and which every creature finds within itself: ﴿He created man from a clinging substance.﴾ The creation of man is among the greatest signs, to the extent that among the creatures we know there is none with more signs than him in his intellect, his perception, and the bonds and bones of his body. "Alaq" is the plural of 'alaqa, which is a small piece of blood. "Al-insan" (man) here is a generic noun, and the mind extends with it to all animals. The reference is not to Adam (peace be upon him), because he was created from clay, and that was not established among those addressed by this verse. Therefore He left aside the origin of creation and brought the branch, which they acknowledge, to bring it closer to their understanding.

(p-653) Then He the Exalted said to him: ﴿Recite, and your Lord is the Most Generous,﴾ in a manner of comfort, as if He the Exalted were saying: "Proceed with what you have been commanded, for your Lord is not like these lords. Rather He is the Most Generous, who is not touched by any deficiency. So He will support you and make you prevail."

Then He enumerated the blessing of the Book by the pen upon people. It is a place of lesson and the greatest benefit in communication and in preserving knowledge. His saying: ﴿He taught man what he did not know﴾ — it was said: the intended one is Muhammad (peace be upon him). It was also said: it is a generic noun, and this is the more apparent. He the Exalted enumerated His blessings: the acquisition of knowledge after ignorance of it.

His saying: ﴿No! Indeed, man...﴾ and the verse: it was revealed after a period concerning Abu Jahl ibn Hisham. He transgressed because of his wealth and the large number of people who frequented his assembly, so he took a hostile stance toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and forbade him from prayer in the mosque. It is narrated that he said: "If I see Muhammad prostrating at the Ka'ba, I will surely step on his neck." It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) answered him and rebuked him. Abu Jahl said: "Does Muhammad threaten me? By Allah, there is no one in the valley with more assembly than me!" He also reported that he came while the Prophet (ﷺ) was praying, and intended to reach him and prevent him from prayer, but then he drew back and left. It was said to him: "What is this?" He said: "A trench of fire stood between me and him, and terror and wings." It is also narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Had he come near me, the angels would have seized him openly." So this surah from His saying "No!" to its end was revealed concerning Abu Jahl. "Kalla" is a rejection of Abu Jahl's sayings and actions, and it may be taken to mean "truly," in which case it is an affirmation of what follows in speech. "Tughyan" (transgression) is going beyond the praiseworthy limits, and "ghina" (wealth) makes one transgress except those whom Allah protects. The pronoun in "ra'ahu" (p-654) refers to the mentioned man, as if He said: "when he sees himself wealthy." This is a sight of the heart which approaches knowledge. Likewise it is permissible for the action of the doer to apply to himself, as you say: "I found myself" and "I considered myself," but you do not say: "I struck myself." The majority recited "an ra'ahu" with a long vowel, on the pattern of "ra'aahu," and they differed about imala (vowel inclination) and its omission. Ibn Kathir, through the transmission of Qunbul, recited "an ra'ahu" without a long vowel, on the pattern of "ra'ahu," by dropping the final radical of the verb, and this is a lightening.

Then He the Exalted belittled this man's wealth and state with His saying: ﴿Indeed, to your Lord is the return,﴾ that is, the gathering and resurrection on the Day of Resurrection. "Ruj'a" is a verbal noun like "ruju'" (return), and is on the pattern of "'uqba" and similar. In this report is a warning to the tyrants among people.

The one who forbids is Abu Jahl, and the servant who prays is Muhammad (ﷺ). His saying: "Have you seen" (ara'ayta) is an interrogation, and it is a verb which does not take two objects in the manner of seeing in the sense of knowing, but is limited to one. His saying: ﴿Does he not know that Allah sees?﴾ completes the rebuke and warning according to the three interrogations. Each one suits each of them, so He brought them in sequence, then brought a warning sufficient for all of them, in brevity and concision. With each of the three affirmations there is an implied complement, in which the expressions can be extended, and His saying "Does he not know" indicates it and suffices. His saying: "If he is" means the praying servant. His saying: ﴿If he denies and turns away﴾ means the man who forbids. He ascribed seeing to Allah the Exalted with the meaning: He perceives the deeds of all with a perception which He called seeing. Allah the Exalted is exempt from having a body part and from all resemblance to originated things. Then He the Exalted threatened him, if he does not desist, that he will be seized by his forelock and dragged to Hell in humiliation. The Arabs say: "I seized the forelock of the horse, or its foot," when you pull it, subduing it. 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib said:

A people who, when they hear the cry, you see them between one who bridles his mare and one who seizes her by the forelock.

So the verse is like His saying: ﴿They will be seized by the forelocks and the feet﴾ [al-Rahman: 41]. Some scholars said, in explaining "la-nasfa'an": it means "we will surely burn," from their saying: "The fire scorched him" when it burned him. "Al-nasiya" is the front part of the hair of the head. Then He the Exalted replaced the indefinite with the definite in His saying: ﴿a lying forelock,﴾ and described it as lying and sinning, in terms of being an attribute of its owner, as you say: "a thieving hand."

His saying: ﴿Then let him call his assembly﴾ is an allusion to the saying of Abu Jahl: "There is no one in the valley with more assembly than me." "Al-nadi" and "al-nada" mean the gathering place, and from it comes "Dar al-Nadwa," and from it the saying of Zuhayr:

And among them are fine standing places, their faces, and gatherings which speech and action frequent.

And from it the saying of the Bedouin woman: "The lord of his assembly, and the protector of his dependents."

"Al-zabaniya" are the angels of punishment. Their singular is "zabaniya." Al-Kisa'i said: "zibni." 'Isa ibn 'Umar al-Akhfash said: "zabin." They are those who push people into the fire. "Al-zabn" is pushing, and from it "harb zabun" (a fierce war), meaning it pushes people into itself. From it the saying of the poet:

And one amazed at what he sees of our moaning, and even if war pushed him he would not stumble.

And from it the saying of 'Utba ibn Abi Sufyan: "War has pushed us and we pushed it; so we are its sons and it is our mother." And from it the saying of the poet:

The enemies have kept me from visiting you, and a fierce war has come between us.

The waw was dropped from "sanad'u" in the script of the Mushaf for brevity and lightness. The meaning: "We will call the zabaniya to punish this one who calls his assembly." Ibn Mas'ud recited: "fal-yad'u ila nadihi."

Then He the Exalted said to Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿No!﴾ as a rejection of the words and deeds of this disbeliever. ﴿Do not obey him,﴾ that is, do not turn to his prohibition and his speech. ﴿But prostrate﴾ to your Lord, ﴿and draw near﴾ to Him by your prostration, by obedience, and by righteous deeds. In a hadith, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The closest a servant is to his Lord is when he prostrates, so increase supplication in prostration, for it is likely to be answered for you." Mujahid said: "Have you not heard: 'prostrate and draw near'?" Ibn Wahb related from a group of the people of knowledge that His saying "prostrate" is addressed to Muhammad (ﷺ), and that "draw near" is addressed to Abu Jahl, meaning: if you are bold enough, see how you will perish.

This surah contains a prostration according to a group of the people of knowledge, among them Ibn Wahb, a companion of Malik.

The tafsir of Surat [al-Qalam] is complete, and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

The enemies have kept me from visiting you, and a fierce war has come between us.

The waw was dropped from "sanad'u" in the script of the Mushaf for brevity and lightness. The meaning: "We will call the zabaniya to punish this one who calls his assembly." Ibn Mas'ud recited: "fal-yad'u ila nadihi."

Then He the Exalted said to Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿No!﴾ as a rejection of the words and deeds of this disbeliever. ﴿Do not obey him,﴾ that is, do not turn to his prohibition and his speech. ﴿But prostrate﴾ to your Lord, ﴿and draw near﴾ to Him by your prostration, by obedience, and by righteous deeds. In a hadith, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The closest a servant is to his Lord is when he prostrates, so increase supplication in prostration, for it is likely to be answered for you." Mujahid said: "Have you not heard: 'prostrate and draw near'?" Ibn Wahb related from a group of the people of knowledge that His saying "prostrate" is addressed to Muhammad (ﷺ), and that "draw near" is addressed to Abu Jahl, meaning: if you are bold enough, see how you will perish.

This surah contains a prostration according to a group of the people of knowledge, among them Ibn Wahb, a companion of Malik.

The tafsir of Surat [al-Qalam] is complete, and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
